_metadata.scope: every structural ancestor above the item level, up to the whole work; partial where descendants lack interpretations (see each entry's _metadata.partial and coverage)

pl-l1d37.summary: Lombard's treatment of the ways God is in things, arising as a digression from the discussion of divine knowledge and whether things are 'in God'. He establishes that God is everywhere by essence, presence, and power, yet dwells only in the good by grace (c1-3), defends divine purity against contamination by things (c4), and then argues that God is neither local nor temporal and changes by neither place nor time (c5-9). To this end he distinguishes bodily locality (dimension plus place-definition) from created spirits' locality (place-definition only) and from God's complete non-locality, answering the objection that God's coming to be in new creatures implies change.
claims: God is essentially, presentially, and potentially in all things without limitation or change.
God dwells by grace only in the good, and in Christ by the grace of union.
God's presence to things does not defile him (simplicity and purity).
God is neither circumscribed nor moved by place or time; created spirits are local in a qualified sense, bodies wholly so.
God's beginning to be in new creatures implies no change in God.
The mode of God's essential omnipresence exceeds human comprehension.

pl-l2d44.summary: Lombard asks about the source of the power to sin and the duty of resistance to power. He argues against those who assign the power of evil to humans or the devil that all power, even power to do harm, comes from God, with culpability lying in the will and in proud misuse (c1); he then reconciles this with Romans 13 by holding that resistance to any power commanding against God is obedience to God's ordination (c2).
claims: The power of sinning or harming is from God, though the will to do so is not.
Culpability lies in the abuse of power, not in power itself.
Romans 13 concerns lawful secular power; commands against God must be resisted.
Resisting a contra-divine command is obedience to the divine ordering.

pl-liber1.summary: Partial summary of Book 1 (on the Trinity and God), based only on Distinction 37. There Lombard treats how God is in things: essentially, presentially, and potentially in all things yet by grace only in the good, undefiled by creatures, and neither local nor temporal, as part of the doctrine of divine attributes and knowledge. The remaining distinctions of Book 1 have not yet been interpreted, so this entry does not represent the whole book.
claims: God is omnipresent by essence, presence, and power without locality or change.
God's indwelling is by grace and differs from his universal presence.

pl-liber2.summary: Partial summary of Book 2 (on creation and sin), based only on Distinction 44. There Lombard argues that all power, including the power to sin or harm, is from God while the guilt lies in the will's abuse of it, and that resisting a power that commands against God is obedience to God's ordering. The remaining distinctions of Book 2 have not yet been interpreted, so this entry does not represent the whole book.
claims: The power to sin is from God; the evil lies in the will and its misuse.
Power commanding against God must be resisted, which is obedience to God.

pl-l3d23.summary: Lombard opens the treatise on the theological virtues by asking whether Christ, full of grace, also had faith and hope, and answers by first giving a full account of faith. Faith is the virtue by which unseen things pertaining to religion are believed. 'Faith' is said in three ways: formed faith (a virtue, informed by charity), unformed faith (a real quality of mind and gift of God, but no virtue, which demons and bad Christians have), and the content believed. Using Augustine's triad, he separates believing God exists and believing God's word, which the wicked can do, from believing into God, which loves and adheres to him and justifies. When charity comes, the unformed quality probably remains and becomes a virtue. Faith is one in content for all but one only in kind as a habit. It properly concerns only the non-apparent, yet is seen intellectually by its possessor. Expounding Hebrews 11:1, faith is the substance and foundation of hoped-for goods and the proof of unseen things. The act of faith naturally precedes hope and charity, though charity, being the Holy Spirit and mother of the virtues, is the cause of faith as a virtue, not its effect. To believe is to think with assent.
claims: Faith is the virtue by which unseen things pertaining to religion are believed.
Faith is said as formed virtue, as unformed quality, and as content believed.
Only believing into God, which includes love and adherence, justifies; believing that God exists or that his word is true is shared by the wicked.
Unformed faith is a real quality and gift of God which likely becomes a virtue when charity arrives.
Faith is numerically one as content, but one only by likeness as a habit.
Faith properly concerns only the non-apparent, though it is itself known intellectually by its possessor.
Faith is the foundation of all virtues and good works, but not of charity, which causes it.
The act of faith naturally, not temporally or causally, precedes the acts of hope and charity.

pl-l3d24.summary: Lombard defends and refines the thesis that faith concerns only what is unseen. Against John 14:29 he argues with Augustine that seen things only prompt belief in unseen things, as Thomas saw flesh and believed God; ordinary talk of believing one's eyes is improper, and the heavenly 'faith of things' is not faith but its reward. Peter's faith in the passion lay not in believing that a man suffered, which he saw, but that God suffered; the merit of faith lies in believing the God-man died. Finally, faith is not about the wholly unknown: it is not of objects of bodily sight but can concern what interior vision grasps. Some things must be understood to be believed, others believed to be understood; faith comes from hearing, purifies the heart, and increases understanding, so that what is believed is partly but not wholly unknown, as one can love what one does not fully know. Perfect knowledge of God awaits the next life.
claims: Faith properly concerns only the unseen; visible things merely occasion belief in invisible ones.
The beatific 'faith of things' is not properly faith but its reward.
Faith in the passion consists in believing that the one who suffered is God.
Faith concerns objects of interior, not exterior, vision and is never about the wholly unknown.
Some truths must be understood before belief, others believed before understanding.
Faith purifies the heart and increases understanding, while perfect knowledge awaits the next life.

pl-l3d25.summary: Lombard turns to the sufficiency of faith for salvation across history. Faith has grown over time in knowledge and articles, and while Hebrews 11:6 (believing that God exists and rewards) is a necessary minimum, it never sufficed: from Adam's fall onward no one has been saved without faith in the Mediator, the ancients believing in future what we believe as past. Not everyone needed explicit knowledge: revelation was distinct for the greater (Abraham, Moses) and veiled for the simple, who believed implicitly by adhering to the greater, as less capable Christians now hold the Creed. Lombard reports, without deciding between them, opinions on the minimum the ancients had to believe about Christ (four articles, or the Son's birth and judgment given faith in the Trinity). He resolves the case of Cornelius, who believed in the incarnation without knowing it had occurred, with Peter sent to announce it and baptize. He closes by holding with Gregory that faith, hope, charity, and works are equal in intensity in this life, while charity is greater because it endures and mothers the virtues; it is said to 'proceed' from faith and hope only because it never exists without them.
claims: Belief that God exists and rewards is necessary but never sufficient for salvation.
No one before or after Christ has been saved without faith in the Mediator.
The ancients and moderns share one faith differing only in tense.
Revelation may be distinct (explicit) or veiled (implicit); the simple are saved by implicit faith adhering to the greater.
Cornelius had faith in the incarnation without knowing it had been fulfilled.
Faith, hope, charity, and works are equal in intensity in this life, but charity is greater.
Charity does not arise from faith and hope but presupposes them.

pl-liber3.summary: Partial summary of Book 3 (on the incarnation, the virtues, and the commandments), based only on Distinctions 23 to 25, the opening of the treatise on the theological virtues. There Lombard defines faith as the virtue by which unseen religious truths are believed; distinguishes formed from unformed faith and the act from the content of faith; separates believing God, believing God's word, and believing into God; treats faith as the foundation of the virtues while making charity its cause; argues that faith concerns only what is unseen yet is not about the wholly unknown, and that faith and understanding mutually advance; and holds that faith in the Mediator, explicit or implicit, has always been necessary for salvation. The prologue and the other 37 distinctions, including the Christology of Distinctions 1 to 22, have not yet been interpreted, so this entry does not represent the whole book.
claims: Faith is the virtue of believing unseen religious truths, formed by charity into a virtue.
Charity is the cause and mother of the virtues, including faith.
Faith concerns the unseen but is never about the wholly unknown, and it advances understanding.
Faith in the Mediator, explicit or implicit, has always been necessary for salvation.

lombardsententia.summary: Very partial summary of Peter Lombard's Sentences, based only on Liber 1 (Distinction 37), Liber 2 (Distinction 44), and Liber 3 (Distinctions 23 to 25); Liber 4 has no interpretations yet. The interpreted portions show Lombard's method of assembling and harmonizing patristic and scriptural authorities, chiefly Augustine and Gregory, to resolve questions: God's non-local, immutable, grace-indwelling presence in creation (Book 1); God's sovereignty over all power together with the moral limits of obedience (Book 2); and the nature of faith, its relation to charity and understanding, and its necessity for salvation in every age (Book 3).
claims: Lombard resolves questions by collating and harmonizing patristic and scriptural authorities, chiefly Augustine.
Divine causality of power and divine immutable presence are maintained alongside creaturely responsibility and distinction.
Faith formed by charity, whether explicit or implicit, is necessary for salvation, and charity is the mother of the virtues.
